# Does a reset ansatz beat barren plateaus on ibm_phoenix?

Literature check, four candidate ansätze, exact simulation to 12 qubits, hardware costing, and odds. Frank by request.

**Verdict: the breakthrough as framed does not survive.** All three legs of the starting claim fail against the literature, and the simulation shows why: resets cut the light cone, which anti-concentrates the cost while making every parameter more than a few layers from the output untrainable, and the surviving circuit is exactly what Pauli propagation simulates best. What does survive is a well-posed hardware test nobody has run (Section 6). Odds that the original idea yields a PRX Quantum/Quantum paper: about 5%. Odds for the reframed test as a stand-alone paper: 10 to 15%; as an arm of Paper 1: 70%.

## 1. The starting claim against the literature

**Leg 1: "Mele et al. exclude measurement-and-reset."** Only half true. Mele et al. (2403.13927, Nat. Phys. 2026) model noise as one single-qubit channel N on every qubit after every 2-design layer, parametrised by c = (‖D‖² + ‖t‖²)/3. Reset to |0⟩ is amplitude damping with γ = 1: t = (0,0,1), D = 0, c = 1/3. Theorem 1 (effective log depth) and Proposition 3 (the classical estimator) need only c &lt; 1, so they cover reset. Theorem 5 (Θ(1) variance of local costs) assumes only non-unital noise with ‖t‖₂ = Θ(1) and so formally covers reset too. Theorem 8 and Corollary 9 (Var\[∂C\] = exp(−Θ(L−k)); Θ(1) gradient norm) are the ones that exclude a replacer channel, stated in the paper as noise that "does not output a fixed state". The reason for that exclusion is ours to state, not theirs: a channel with a fixed output erases every derivative upstream of it, so a full-register reset makes the bound vacuous. What their theorems do not cover is reset on a *subset* of qubits per layer. That is the only genuine gap, and it is the case simulated below. Singkanipa and Lidar (2402.08721, Quantum 2025) define HS-contractive non-unital maps by ‖N(ρ₁)−N(ρ₂)‖₂ ≤ r‖ρ₁−ρ₂‖₂; reset is the r = 0 member, inside their framework, and they extend the parameter-shift rule to noisy channels, which we can cite for gradient validity.

**Leg 2: "No trainability result for dissipative or measurement-based ansätze."** False. The table lists what exists. The decisive item is Shirgure, Kökcü and Niu (2606.23751, June 2026): with purification and Pauli-path analysis they show that feedforward, reset and engineered-dissipation gadgets anti-concentrate the cost through Pauli terms supported on ancillas whose coefficients depend only on gadget parameters, while upstream parameters stay exponentially untrainable; their conclusion, argued through Stinespring purification rather than proved as a theorem, is that building a barren-plateau-free dynamic circuit is at least as hard as building a barren-plateau-free unitary ansatz from first principles.

**Leg 3: "No simulability result covers mid-circuit reset."** False, and reset is the easiest case. In the Heisenberg picture the reset adjoint maps Z → I, X → 0, Y → 0: Pauli weight can only fall. Angrisani, Mele et al. (2501.13101, PRX Quantum 2026) prove Pauli propagation efficient for any local noise including amplitude damping with γ ∈ (0, 1\], i.e. including reset, and state that their results also cover dynamic non-unitary operations of the Deshpande type when applied at a constant rate; Martinez et al. (2501.13050, PRL 2025) prove the same for Pauli backpropagation under non-unital noise; Deshpande et al. themselves note that, with high probability over the initial parameters, their dynamic circuits are efficiently simulable by low-weight Pauli-path propagation. The correct statement of what is open is narrower than the programme's claim: reset circuits at random initialisation are simulable on average; structured reset circuits can be hard (Angrisani et al. point to the quantum-refrigerator scheme as an engineered non-unital circuit that is not simulable, and Fefferman et al., 2306.16659, PRX Quantum 2024, show non-unital noise removes anti-concentration at every depth, with consequences for both hardness and easiness); and a circuit that is trainable at random initialisation is, by construction, one that sits near the average case. That is the Cerezo et al. dichotomy, not an escape from it.

| arXiv | Year | Claim relevant to Paper 2 | Effect |

No reset or dynamic ansatz in this list has been run on hardware; the only gradient-landscape hardware measurement at scale is Schmitt et al. (a gradient-norm proxy on a unitary ansatz). All texts are open on arXiv.

## 2. Candidate ansätze on phoenix (CZ + per-qubit reset, 2×W patches)

All use RY·RZ on every qubit (2 parameters per qubit per layer), then CZ on every patch edge (three parallel sublayers: even and odd horizontal pairs, vertical pairs). Cost is ⟨Z<sub>d0</sub>Z<sub>d1</sub>⟩ on an adjacent data pair in row 0. Parameter shift with ±π/2 stays exact for channels: the cost is affine in the superoperator of each gate, so it is a + b cos θ + c sin θ in any single angle whatever the resets do (Singkanipa–Lidar give the noisy-channel version).

### (i) Dissipative HEA, checkerboard

At the start of layers 2..L reset the qubits with (row + col + ℓ) even: every qubit is reset every second layer.

- **params**: 2nL
- **native depth / layer**: 2 sx + 3 CZ + reset
- **light cone**: uncut, but paths suppressed at e<sup>−3.3</sup> per layer (§3)

### (ii) Dissipative HEA, random half

Fixed pseudo-random half of the qubits reset each layer; the observed data pair is never reset.

- **params**: 2nL
- **native depth / layer**: 2 sx + 3 CZ + reset
- **light cone**: pruned Pauli paths; survives only along never-reset chains

### (iii) Ancilla-row reset

Row 0 data, row 1 ancilla; ancilla row measured and reset after every layer (Zapusek-type; on phoenix, one reset element per qubit).

- **params**: 2nL (nL on data)
- **native depth / layer**: 2 sx + 3 CZ + measure/reset
- **light cone**: full along the data row; ancilla legs cut each layer

(iv) Feedforward (Deshpande-type: RX on the data neighbour conditioned on the ancilla outcome) is a superset of (iii); every simulability argument above applies to it and 2606.23751 treats it directly, so it was not simulated.

**What the scalings would mean.** Θ(1) early-layer variance in n and L would be a genuine escape and, per Cerezo et al. (2312.09121), would demand a simulability check. Polynomial decay would match Zapusek's bound. Exponential decay in the distance to the output at a constant rate α (Mele's Theorem 8 form) is what the light-cone argument predicts: a Pauli path reaching an early parameter must never carry X or Y on a qubit at the moment it is reset, each reset layer removes a constant fraction of paths, and the cost depends only on the last Θ(1/α) layers, which Pauli propagation handles with a smaller path budget than the noiseless circuit.

## 3. Simulation

Exact, noiseless, ensemble-statevector simulation with explicit trace-and-replace resets (cross-checked against qiskit-aer density matrices to 1e-10), n = 4..12 on 2×W patches, L = 1..8, M = 200 uniform parameter draws, ±π/2 parameter-shift gradients of ⟨Z<sub>d0</sub>Z<sub>d1</sub>⟩ with respect to the RY on d0 in the first layer (k = 1), the middle layer (k = ⌈L/2⌉) and the last layer (k = L), bootstrap 95% CIs (2000 resamples). Total compute 44 CPU-minutes on 4 shared cores. Files: paper2/paper2_gradvar_results.csv, paper2/sim2.py.

| dissipative HEA, checkerboard | 2.7e-11 \[5.8e-13, 7.5e-11\] | 8.7e-07 | 1.24e-01 | 4534574905.3 | 1.46e-01 | 2.64 / 6 | 3.34 (L=3..8) · 3.42 (L=5..8) |

**Headlines.** At n = 12, L = 8 the first-layer variance is 1.21e-03 for the plain HEA, 8.3e-04 for the random-half dissipative HEA, 2.9e-04 for the ancilla-row reset and 2.7e-11 for the checkerboard. No reset variant is above the plain HEA at any n or L in the grid; the ancilla-row reset is below it by 5.7x at n = 4, 5.2x at n = 6, 4.0x at n = 8, 7.2x at n = 10, 4.2x at n = 12 (first-layer parameter), and by similar factors for the last-layer parameter and for Var\[C\]. **The k-profile is flat.** At L = 8 the ratio Var\[∂C\] last layer / first layer is 1.6 / 2.3 / 1.5 / 4.3 / 3.6 for the ancilla-row reset (n = 4, 6, 8, 10, 12), 2.4 / 2.3 / 2.6 / 2.2 / 2.3 for the HEA and 1.6 / 4.7 / 1.4 / 4.5 / 2.0 for the random half; the mid-layer point sits between (table). A Mele Theorem 8 profile would put the last layer at Θ(1) with the first layer exponentially below it, a ratio growing like e<sup>0.8·7</sup> ≈ 300 at these rates; the measured ratios are 1 to 5. **What decays is everything, with L.** At n = 8 the ancilla-row reset's Var\[C\] falls at 0.66 per layer, its last-layer variance at 0.70 and its first-layer variance at 0.74 (fit L = 3..8; the HEA's Var\[C\] falls at 0.38), all toward the Haar value 1/(2<sup>n</sup>+1) ≈ 3.9e-3 for n = 8. That is ordinary depth-driven concentration of a small 2×W patch, the same for every ansatz, not a non-unital layer-index profile. The checkerboard is the exception only because its observed pair is reset within two layers of the output (below). The resets did not fight the plateau here; on this patch they added nothing that a shallower unitary circuit would not.

**Why (i) looks two layers deep.** Backward from the output, Z<sub>d0</sub> passes through the CZ layer unchanged and the rotation turns it into cos θ Z + sin θ X on d0. By construction d0 is reset before layer L and d1 before layer L−1, so Z → I and X, Y → 0 on the observed pair within two layers, and the cost is, to leading order, a function of the last two layers' angles. The light cone is not cut (the cone reaches layer 1 at every L in the table) and no gradient is identically zero (frac_exact_zero ≤ 1 in 200 draws for every parameter): the surviving Pauli paths, those where an X first spread a Z onto a neighbour through CZ and the next rotation turned the origin's X into a Z before its reset, are suppressed at e<sup>−3.3</sup> per layer (fit L = 3..8 at n = 8: e<sup>−3.3</sup>; L = 4..8 at n = 12: e<sup>−2.7</sup>), so by L = 8 the first-layer variance is 1e-10 to 1e-11, dead for any shot budget. The large Var\[C\] (Var\[C\] = 0.15 at n = 12) is trivial by observable placement: a depth-2 function of a few angles has O(1) variance, and comparing it with a depth-8 HEA says nothing about the plateau.

**What was cut and why.** The grid is n = 4..12 at L = 8, L = 1..8 at n = 8, and L = 4 at n = 12; the n = 12 depth scan (L = 1..7) was dropped on the coordinator's time check, so α<sub>L</sub> at n = 12 is a two-point estimate and the fitted rates are quoted at n = 8 with their fit range. The mid-layer parameter was added in the rerun after review. The feedforward variant (iv) was not simulated. Everything is noiseless: reset error, readout error and T1 during a 2 µs measure-based reset are not in the model.

## 4. The simulability trade-off

The data-row entropy (bottom right of the figure) says the ancilla-reset ansatz delivers a data row that is nearly maximally mixed (5.83 of 6 bits at n = 12), i.e. the resets act on the data row as strong non-unital noise, the regime of Mele's Theorem 1. The checkerboard ansatz keeps the state purer (2.64 bits) because it never lets entanglement build. Neither direction is favourable: mixed means noise-simulable, pure-and-shallow means light-cone-simulable. The honest proxy is the Pauli-path budget, and with the reset rule Z → I, X/Y → 0 that budget is strictly smaller than for the same circuit without resets. The Cerezo et al. dichotomy is not evaded here; it is illustrated.

**One loophole, weak but real.** Every simulability theorem above assumes independent layers. A parameter-shared Floquet dissipative ansatz (Dowarah et al., 2605.30572: one parametrised layer repeated, so the deep circuit is a fixed channel iterated to its fixed point) makes every parameter a last-layer parameter, and the gradient becomes a derivative of the channel's fixed point, which Theorem 8 does not address. It is still a shallow-effective-circuit story (the fixed point is reached in O(1/α) iterations and is what Pauli propagation converges to), so I rate it as unlikely to yield hardness, but it is the one variant a referee could say we did not test.

## 5. Sharpest testable hypothesis

**H2 (two parts).** On ibm_phoenix, for the ancilla-row reset ansatz (iii) and a gate-count-matched plain HEA on 2×W patches, W = 6 and 10, L = 4 and 8, with parameter-shift variances at k = 1 and k = L over 200 draws: **(a) depth decay.** Var\[C\], Var\[∂<sub>k=1</sub>C\] and Var\[∂<sub>k=L</sub>C\] all fall between L = 4 and L = 8 at a common rate for both ansätze (simulation, n = 8, fit L = 3..8: α<sub>L</sub> = 0.74 for the reset ansatz, 0.47 for the HEA); the reset ansatz is never above the HEA. **(b) layer-index profile.** At L = 8 the ratio Var\[∂<sub>k=L</sub>C\] / Var\[∂<sub>k=1</sub>C\] is below 10 for both ansätze (simulation at n = 12: 3.6 reset, 2.3 HEA), i.e. there is no Θ(1) last layer over an exponentially suppressed first layer. A Pauli propagation with the reset rule Z → I, X/Y → 0 truncated at weight 6 reproduces all 8 hardware points within their bootstrap CIs after readout mitigation.

**Falsifier** (any one, at two or more points, outside the bootstrap CI): the reset ansatz's Var\[∂<sub>k=1</sub>C\] above the matched HEA's; a k = L / k = 1 ratio above 10 for the reset ansatz at L = 8; Var\[C\] of the reset ansatz flat in L while the HEA's falls; ~~or a Pauli-propagation residual outside the CI. Any of these would be the interesting outcome and would reopen the question.~~ \[Struck 19 Sep 2026 after theorist review: a truncation residual does not imply hardness; average-case simulability is proven (Angrisani et al. 2501.13101).\] Prediction, frankly: none fires.

A first hardware measurement of a dynamic-circuit gradient landscape and a direct test of anti-concentration-without-trainability at 20 to 100 qubits: not a breakthrough, a clean falsification test with a classical baseline, which is what Question 3 of the decision memo should become.

## 6. Hardware experiment and cost

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Qubits | Six disjoint 2×10 strips (rows 0–1, 2–3, … 10–11) give W = 10 patches in parallel; W = 6 by truncation. Exclude qubit 17 (dead) and the 7 qubits with readout error &gt; 3e-2 from data rows. |
| Depths and parameters | L = 4 and 8; gradient parameters at k = 1 and k = L (first and last layer). The mid-layer point is measured in simulation only. |
| Arm size | 8 points: 2 W (6 and 10) × 2 L × 2 ansätze (ancilla-row reset, gate-count-matched plain HEA), M = 200 draws × (2 params × 2 shifts + 1) = 1000 circuits per point, 4096 shots, sharing Paper 1's calibration snapshots and readout mitigation. No 16k-shot points: the predicted first-layer variance at n = 12, L = 8 (2.9e-04) is above the 4096-shot floor of 1.2e-4, and anything below it is dropped rather than bought with shots. |
| Circuit time | Per layer: 80 ns (two sx, rz virtual) + 204 ns (three CZ sublayers at 68 ns) + reset. Measure-based reset costs 1940 ns readout plus feedforward latency, so 2.3 to 2.5 µs per layer; a bare dissipative reset should be sub-microsecond (the r2 blog quotes an effective T1 of 25 ns) but its duration is not in the calibration CSV and must be measured in the dry run. L = 8: 3 µs (bare reset) to 21 µs (measure-based), plus 1.94 µs readout. |
| QPU minutes per point | **Headline, IBM default rep_delay ≈ 250 µs:** 1000 circuits × 4096 shots × (250 + 24) µs ≈ 18.7 min of execution, or 24 min by IBM's rule of thumb (2 s + 0.35 ms per execution). **Floor, rep_delay = 1 µs** (the r2 repetition delay, which the flex-plan instance must expose and the dry run must confirm): 1000 × 4096 × 25 µs ≈ 1.7 min, budget 3 to 5 min with overheads. Check job.usage_estimation before submitting and job.usage() after. |
| Kill criteria | Locked time above 5 min per point in the dry run; measure-based reset above 2 µs per layer with no bare reset exposed; reset or init error above 2e-2. If any fires, the arm is dropped and the minutes go to Paper 1's ladder. At the floor the 8-point arm costs 15 to 40 min; at default rep_delay it costs 150 to 190 min and cannot run inside the 180-minute instance alongside Paper 1. |

## 7. Open risks, with odds

| Risk or outcome | Odds |
|---|---|
| The original claim (a reset ansatz trainable at depth and not classically simulable) turns out true in any form we can test. | 5% |
| Hardware reproduces H2(a) and (b) at W = 6 and 10: the common L-decay between L = 4 and 8 for Var\[C\] and both gradient parameters, and a k = L / k = 1 ratio below 10 at L = 8, within CIs. | 65% |
| Reset error or measure-based reset latency pushes the k = 1 point at L = 8 under the 4096-shot floor. | 40% |
| Mid-circuit reset is compiled to measure + conditional X, making the L = 8 points exceed the T1-limited budget. | 35% |
| Another group publishes a hardware DPQC gradient test before mid-October. | 15% |
| Reframed test accepted at PRX Quantum or Quantum as a stand-alone paper. Lowered from an earlier 20–30%: it is a hardware confirmation of a predicted null with a classical baseline, and the simulation shows ordinary depth concentration rather than any non-unital physics, so its natural home is an arm of Paper 1. | 10–15% |
| Reframed test accepted as a section of Paper 1 or a short companion in QST/PRA. | 70% |

**Recommendation.** Do not pre-register Paper 2 as a breakthrough or as a separate paper. Pre-register H2 as the gated Question 3 arm of Paper 1: 8 points, ansatz (iii) against a matched HEA, k = 1 and k = L, 4096 shots, Pauli-propagation baseline with the reset rule, run only if the dry run clears the kill criteria in Section 6. Variant (iv) only if H2 is falsified.

## Review

Reviewed 19 Sept 2026 by an independent adversarial pass (scratchpad/review/paper2_memo_review.md). Changes made in this version: removed a Mele quotation that is not in the paper and corrected the theorem attribution (Theorem 5 covers reset; Theorem 8 and Corollary 9 exclude replacer channels); Shirgure and Deshpande paraphrased instead of quoted; the mid-layer gradient parameter was simulated on the full grid and H2 restated from the measured k-profile with a precise falsifier; the "identically zero gradient" claim replaced by the measured e<sup>−3.3</sup> per-layer suppression and the checkerboard Var\[C\] re-described as trivial by observable placement; "nothing suggests hardness" replaced by the average-case versus structured statement with Fefferman et al.; hardware budget restated at IBM default rep_delay with the 1 µs figure as the floor, a locked-time kill criterion added and the arm cut to 8 points; Schmitt et al. named as the nearest hardware precedent; the parameter-shared Floquet loophole added; stand-alone odds lowered to 10–15%; α fit ranges stated; dissrand added to validate.py (12/12 agree with Aer).

**19 Sep 2026, after the theorist's second opinion** ([theorist_second_opinion](https://claude.ai/artifact/7WLx5wkkAz1f8AYMXxsVJj)): the falsifier clause that treated a Pauli-propagation residual outside the CI as an outcome that would reopen the trainable-and-hard question is struck in place (Section 5). The inference ran the wrong way: disagreement with a truncated classical method is evidence of truncation or noise-model error, never of hardness, because average-case simulability of these circuits is proven (Angrisani et al. 2501.13101). The other three falsifiers stand. No numbers changed.
